{{short description|Game theory problem}}
'''Strategic fair division''' studies problems of [[fair division]], in which participants cooperate to subdivide goods or resources fairly, from a point of view in which the participants are assumed to hide their preferences and act strategically in order to maximize their own utility, rather than playing sincerely according to their true preferences.

To illustrate the difference between strategic fair division and classic fair division, consider the [[divide and choose]] procedure for dividing a cake among two agents. In classic fair division, it is assumed that the cutter cuts the cake into two pieces that are equal in his eyes, and thus he always gets a piece that he values at exactly 1/2 of the total cake value. However, if the cutter knows the chooser's preferences, he can get much more than 1/2 by acting strategically.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Extension of the Classical Rule of "Divide and Choose"|first=Eugene|last=Singer|journal=Southern Economic Journal|date=April 1962|volume=28|issue=4|pages=391–394|doi=10.2307/1055235 |jstor=1055235}}</ref> For example, suppose the cutter values a piece by its size while the chooser values a piece by the amount of chocolate in it. So the cutter can cut the cake into two pieces with almost the same amount of chocolate, such that the smaller piece has slightly more chocolate. Then, the chooser will take the smaller piece and the cutter will win the larger piece, which may be worth much more than 1/2 (depending on how the chocolate is distributed).

The research in strategic fair division has two main branches.

One branch is related to [[game theory]] and studies the equilibria in games created by fair division algorithms:

* The [[Nash equilibrium]] of the Dubins-Spanier moving-knife protocol;<ref>{{Cite conference|last1=Brânzei|first1=Simina|last2=Miltersen|first2=Peter Bro|date=2013|contribution=Equilibrium Analysis in Cake Cutting|contribution-url=https://pure.au.dk/ws/portalfiles/portal/54560937/strategic_dubins_spanier.pdf|title=Proceedings of the 2013 International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multi-agent Systems (AAMAS '13)|location=Richland, SC|publisher=International Foundation for Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems|pages=327–334|isbn=9781450319935}}</ref>
* The Nash equilibrium and [[subgame-perfect equilibrium]] of generalized-cut-and-choose protocols;<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brânzei|first1=Simina|last2=Caragiannis|first2=Ioannis|last3=Kurokawa|first3=David|last4=Procaccia|first4=Ariel D.|title=An Algorithmic Framework for Strategic Fair Division |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |date=2016-02-21 |volume=30 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v30i1.10042 |s2cid=7226490 |language=en|arxiv=1307.2225}}</ref>
* The equilibria of envy-free protocols for allocating an indivisible good with monetary compensations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tadenuma|first1=Koichi|last2=Thomson|first2=William|date=1995-05-01|title=Games of Fair Division|journal=Games and Economic Behavior|volume=9|issue=2|pages=191–204|doi=10.1006/game.1995.1015|issn=0899-8256|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*The [[price of anarchy]] of Nash equilibria of two mechanisms for homogeneous-resource allocation: the [[Fisher market]] game and the Trading Post game.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Brânzei|first1=Simina|last2=Gkatzelis|first2=Vasilis|last3=Mehta|first3=Ruta|date=2016-07-06|title=Nash Social Welfare Approximation for Strategic Agents|eprint=1607.01569|class=cs.GT}}</ref>

The other branch is related to [[mechanism design]] and aims to find [[truthful mechanism]]s for fair division, in particular:

*[[Truthful cake-cutting]];
*[[Truthful resource allocation]];
*[[Rental harmony#Strategic considerations|Truthful fair division of rooms and rent]].
